When and Where?

Roguelike Celebration 2026 will be held on Saturday and Sunday October 17 – October 18, 2026 as a virtual event in our custom-built multiplayer game/chat space. Talks will also be streamed to Twitch and YouTube.

Our call for presenters closed on July 19, 2026. We will respond to all submissions by mid-August.

There will also be a free preview event September 13, 2026 in the same social space, with talks streamed to Twitch and YouTube:

  • “Ancient Roguelikes: The Pre-History of Roguelike Games” by Martin Pichlmair
  • “Bitwise Black Magic: How to Computer, Better Faster Stronger” by Greg L
  • “Don’t Save The @: What Roguelikes Teach Us About Story Structure” by Jamie Brittain

Check back here for more details and a schedule as the event approaches.

Get Updates

For updates leading up to the conference, you can sign up to our mailing list.

14:15 21:15 T Ancient Roguelikes: The Pre-History of Roguelike Games
Roguelikes existed before Rogue. How can that be? This talk takes you on a worldwide journey back in time to ancient forms of procedural generation, tracing some roots of the games we play nowadays.		 Martin Pichlmair
14:45 21:45 T Bitwise Black Magic: How to Computer, Better Faster Stronger
There’s a famous wtf moment in Quake 3 Arena’s source code, involving the use of “evil floating point bit level hacking”… but what is that? Hidden inside computer math are a secret set of tools that can help your game run much faster, if you learn the magic behind all of those magic numbers. This talk will be a theme park ride through some of the most impressive optimization techniques I’ve found or created myself, so math enthusiasts at any level can learn something new. Whether it’s using only 1 bit of save data per collectible in huge, randomly generated maps, or using x&-x to instantly find pixel gaps for things like fluid simulations, the hidden math of computers lets you accomplish much more than you probably think!		 Greg L
15:15 22:15 T Don’t Save The @: What Roguelikes Teach Us About Story Structure
As someone who has worked in tv, film - and now AAA gaming, I have long been obsessed with story structures, both as a tool to use in my own work, but also as perhaps the biggest grift in the creative industries today. The Hero With A Thousand Faces, Robert McKee’s Story, Dan Harmon’s ‘story wheel’, and perhaps most of all, Blake Snyder’s ‘Save The Cat’ all contain much wisdom, but they have also contributed to the mass homogenisation of storytelling across culture. How many times have you been reading a book, watching a movie, playing a game, and have found that you know precisely what is going to happen next, and after that, and after that…

I would like to look at how the stories we experience in roguelike games resist the predictability of story structure orthodoxy. Permadeath, random level generation, ascii graphics and turn based gameplay could all be viewed as antithetical to a gripping narrative structure, but, as anyone who has played one of these games knows, they can create some of the most immersive and emotional experiences we can have with games. I will argue that roguelikes teach us about the importance of avoiding well travelled paths (and structures) when we tell stories.		 Jamie Brittain
